Scenario · GE16

Hung by design

Malaysia's 16th general election ended in a three-way tie. Specific groups of voters made it happen, and a handful of leaders will now decide what it produces.

Seats and share of the vote, big three blocs

Changes from GE15

Three ways to 112

Each dot is one seat. Layout is illustrative.

Each dot is one seat. Vote shares are rounded.

Each dot is one seat. Grey: held at GE15, lost. Outlined: gained since GE15.

Hollow dots: the same smaller seats, which can join only one bloc at a time.

PH 62. PN 62. BN 60. Three blocs finished within two seats of one another in a 222-seat parliament. A government needs 112. None of them is close.

BN took the smallest share of the vote, about 28%, yet won almost as many seats as its rivals. The outcome was driven by where votes landed, not how many were cast. BN's support sits in mixed seats won on a split vote. PH piles up huge majorities in urban seats that count no more than a narrow win.

Start from 2022. At GE15, PH won 82 seats, PN 74 and BN 30. Four groups of voters made different choices this time, and each choice pushed seats the same way.

Even with Sarawak, Sabah and every smaller party, a single bloc tops out around 100 seats. A government needs two of the three big blocs, or one of them has to split. PH and PN are the least compatible pair, so BN sits in almost every credible majority.

Anwar Ibrahim will claim the first attempt at forming a government on PH's lead in the vote. He will offer UMNO posts and seat arrangements to keep it away from PAS, but resist any public concession on prosecutions.

Ahmad Zahid Hamidi will negotiate with PH and PN at the same time, and he will take his time, because either choice splits UMNO. He will present the final decision as forced on him by the “fresh mandate” argument he has already made.

Abdul Hadi Awang will push for an UMNO-PAS partnership. He will trade the premiership for state autonomy and the religious and education portfolios, but refuse seat deals that cost PAS seats it already holds.

Muhyiddin Yassin will threaten separate talks with PH or UMNO. Bersatu's 20 seats are his only leverage in a PN that PAS now leads, and BN plus PAS alone reaches only 101.

Abang Johari Openg and Hajiji Noor will wait until BN has chosen. Then they will back whichever grouping offers Borneo the most devolution, and formally defer to the Agong.

BN's ability to join either rival gives it leverage over a result in which it took the smallest share of the vote. Which of these three deals forms depends mainly on three things: whether Zahid can hold UMNO's divided base, whether Hadi accepts being the junior partner, and whether Muhyiddin defects.
